sections.text:
The tabernacle has just been built at Mount Sinai, and God has come to dwell among his people. Now the question is how a people can live near a holy God. Leviticus is the answer, and it is given in detail.

It covers the offerings (chapters 1 to 7), the priests (8 to 10), what is clean and unclean (11 to 15), and the Day of Atonement (16). Then comes holiness in everyday life (17 to 27). Chapter 19 begins with the heart of it: “You shall be holy; for I, the LORD your God, am holy.” That holiness reaches into the fields. The edges of the harvest are to be left standing: “You shall leave them for the poor and for the foreigner.”

The chapter also gives a command that is short and plain: “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” It comes from this book (19:18), and the refrain of the whole book is the same, that the people are to be holy because the LORD is holy.

The book is set at Mount Sinai, directly after the tabernacle is built. Its name comes from the Levites, the tribe that served at the sanctuary. Much of it is written for priests, which is why it reads like a manual.

Christians read the sacrifices as pointing forward to the death of Christ, an argument the letter to the Hebrews works out at length. Most hold that the food and purity laws no longer bind Christians, pointing to passages such as Mark 7 and Acts 10.

There is real disagreement about which other commands carry over, and about how to tell. The book’s own center is plain: a holy God makes a way for people to live near him.

The book opens with a voice from the tent. The LORD calls to Moses from the Tent of Meeting and tells him what to say to Israel about offerings. The first kind is the burnt offering. If a person brings one from the herd, it must be “a male without defect”, offered at the door of the tent. He lays his hand on its head, and it is accepted for him to make atonement. He kills it before the LORD, the priests sprinkle the blood around the altar, and the animal is skinned, cut up and laid in order on the fire. The priest burns all of it, a pleasant aroma to the LORD. The same pattern holds for a male from the flock. For those who offer birds, turtledoves or young pigeons, the priest burns the bird on the altar.

Leviticus follows directly after Exodus 40, where the glory of God filled the tent; now God speaks from it. Tradition links the book to Moses. The first section, chapters 1 to 7, teaches Israel how to approach God with offerings. The text gives the options of herd, flock or birds, which means that a person could bring what they could afford. Readers differ on what sacrifice means today: many Christians read it with Hebrews 10, and Jewish tradition remembers it in prayer and study.

Not every offering is an animal. The meal offering is a gift of grain. A person brings fine flour, pours oil on it and adds frankincense. The priest takes a handful as a memorial and burns it on the altar as a pleasant aroma, and what remains belongs to Aaron and his sons, a most holy part. The offering can also be baked: unleavened cakes mixed with oil, or wafers anointed with oil, or flour cooked on a griddle or in a pan. No meal offering may be made with yeast, and honey is not burned on the altar either. Every offering is to be seasoned with salt, for “the salt of the covenant of your God” must not be lacking. The chapter ends with the first fruits, fresh heads of grain parched with fire and crushed, with oil and frankincense, part of which the priest burns.

Having described animal offerings in Leviticus 1, the book now describes what comes from fields and kitchens. Ordinary food, flour and oil, becomes a gift to God. The portion for the priests shows how the priesthood was supported. Because the text does not explain why yeast and honey are excluded, readers have offered different guesses, and it is best to say that the reason is not given. Compare Leviticus 6 for more on the meal offering.

The peace offering is the third kind. A person brings a bull or cow, a lamb, or a goat, male or female, without defect. He lays his hand on its head and kills it at the door of the Tent of Meeting, and the priests sprinkle the blood around the altar. The fat that covers the innards, the two kidneys and the cover of the liver are burned on the altar, an offering by fire of a pleasant aroma. For a lamb, the fat tail is included as well. The text calls this the food of the offering, and says plainly that all the fat is the LORD's. The chapter ends with a rule for all generations and all dwellings: “you shall eat neither fat nor blood.”

Leviticus 7 shows that a peace offering is the one where the worshiper shares in a meal, so it is often read as an offering of fellowship or thanks. The chapter itself stays with the rules for the fat, which belongs to the LORD, and the blood. Jewish tradition has treated the rule against eating blood as lasting; many Christians point to Acts 15 when discussing it. Readers differ on how these rules apply today.

This chapter is about sins nobody meant. If anyone sins unintentionally, doing one of the things the LORD has commanded not to be done, the sin is still serious, and there is a way back. The text follows the case upward and downward through the community. If the anointed priest sins so that guilt falls on the people, he brings a young bull. If the whole congregation sins, hidden from them until it is known, the elders lay their hands on a bull. When a ruler sins, he brings a male goat; when one of the common people sins, a female goat or lamb. In each case the offerer lays a hand on the animal and kills it, and the priest puts blood on the horns of the altar. For the priest and the congregation, blood is sprinkled seven times before the veil. The result is stated: the priest makes atonement, and “he will be forgiven.”

The offering here is for sin done without intent. The chapter shows that guilt can be real even when it is unknowing, and it scales the offering to the person's position: leaders bear greater responsibility. The same pattern ends with forgiveness. Readers often compare Hebrews 9 and 10 when reading about blood and atonement, while Jewish readers remember these offerings in the context of Temple service and repentance.

Some wrongs are easy to miss, and this chapter lists them. A witness hears a public call to testify and stays silent. Someone touches an unclean carcass or human uncleanness without knowing it. Someone swears a rash oath. When the person learns of it, “he shall confess that in which he has sinned” and bring an offering for atonement. The cost depends on what the person can pay. A lamb or goat is first, but “If he can’t afford a lamb,” two turtledoves or pigeons will do, and if even that is too much, a tenth of an ephah of fine flour. The chapter then turns to the LORD's holy things. If someone wrongs them unwittingly, he brings a ram and makes restitution, adding a fifth. Even someone who sinned without knowing remains guilty, and brings a ram to the priest to be forgiven.

The chapter keeps together confession, restitution and offerings. The provision for the poor is notable: the law makes room for those who have little, so that forgiveness is not reserved for the wealthy. Mary and Joseph's offering in Luke 2:24 is often connected with this kind of provision. The word for this offering is sometimes translated as guilt offering or trespass offering, and the exact lines between types are explained differently by different readers.

What happens when one person wrongs another? This chapter takes up wrongs against a neighbor: lying about a deposit, taking by robbery or oppression, or finding something lost and swearing falsely about it. The answer has two steps. First the person restores what was taken in full and adds a fifth part more, giving it to its owner on the day he is found guilty. Then he brings a ram as a trespass offering, and the priest makes atonement, and he will be forgiven. After this the chapter gives instructions for the priests. The fire on the altar is to burn all night until morning, and “it shall not go out.” The priest removes the ashes and carries them outside the camp. Then come the rules for the meal offering, the daily offering of Aaron and his sons, and the sin offering, which is to be eaten in a holy place.

Here the offering for a wrong against a neighbor cannot be separated from making it right with the person. Restitution comes first. These are instructions for priests, spoken to Aaron and his sons, and they describe the daily work behind the altar. The fire that must never go out is mentioned again in Leviticus 9, where fire from the LORD consumes the offering. Readers differ on whether the law's picture of restitution applies directly today, but many see its concern for justice as lasting.

The long list of offering laws is finished here. The trespass offering is most holy, killed where the burnt offering is killed, and its fat is burned; the priests eat of it in a holy place. The law of the peace offering follows, with a distinction between a thanksgiving offering, eaten on the day it is offered, and a vow or freewill offering, eaten that day or the next, and burned on the third day. Anyone who eats unclean meat, or eats while unclean, is cut off from his people. The people may not eat fat, of bull, sheep or goat, nor any blood, whether of bird or animal. The priests receive the breast and right thigh as their portion forever. The chapter ends by gathering all the laws of the burnt offering, the meal offering, the sin offering, the trespass offering, the consecration and the peace offering, given “in the wilderness of Sinai.”

This chapter finishes the first section of the book. The phrase cut off from his people is serious, and the text does not spell out exactly what it means; readers have understood it in different ways. The priests' share of the offerings supported their work. The closing note places everything at Sinai, in the same wilderness setting as Exodus 19 and the building of the tent in Exodus 35 to 40.

The words of Leviticus 1 to 7 now become action. At the LORD's command, Moses assembles the whole congregation at the door of the Tent of Meeting and tells them, “This is the thing which the LORD has commanded to be done.” He washes Aaron and his sons, dresses Aaron in the tunic, sash, robe, ephod and breastplate, sets the turban on his head, and fixes the golden plate. He anoints the tabernacle, the altar and its vessels, then pours oil on Aaron's head. A bull is brought for a sin offering, one ram for a burnt offering, and a second ram for the consecration, and its blood goes on the right ear, thumb and great toe of Aaron and his sons. They are told to stay at the door of the tent for seven days, day and night. The chapter ends with their obedience.

This is the ordination that Exodus 28 and 29 planned in detail. Moses acts here as the one who sets Aaron and his sons apart, and the repeated phrase as the LORD commanded Moses shows that the work follows the plan. Readers have long found meaning in the seven days of waiting, which keep the new priests at the tent. It leads straight to Leviticus 9, where their service begins.

On the eighth day Moses calls Aaron, his sons and the elders, and the day of service begins. Aaron first offers a calf as a sin offering for himself, and a ram as a burnt offering. Then he brings the people's offering: a goat for sin, a calf and a lamb for burning, a bull and a ram for peace offerings, and a meal offering. His sons hand him the blood, and he does each step as the LORD commanded. Aaron lifts up his hands toward the people and blesses them. Moses and Aaron go into the Tent of Meeting, come out, and bless the people again, and “the LORD’s glory appeared to all the people.” Fire comes out from before the LORD and consumes the burnt offering and fat on the altar. When the people see it, they shout and fall on their faces.

The glory promised in Exodus 29:43 now appears. Notice that Aaron offers for himself before he offers for the people; the priest is also in need. The fire from the LORD follows the pattern of earlier scenes, and the same kind of fire appears in 1 Kings 18 and 2 Chronicles 7. The next chapter turns suddenly and darkly, and the two chapters are best read together.

Joy turns to horror. Nadab and Abihu, sons of Aaron, take their censers, put fire in them, lay incense on it, and offer what the text calls strange fire before the LORD, which he had not commanded. Fire comes out from before the LORD and devours them, and they die. Moses tells Aaron that the LORD said he would show himself holy to those who come near him. And “Aaron held his peace.” Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp, and Moses tells Aaron and his other sons not to mourn in the usual ways, for the anointing oil is on them. The LORD then speaks to Aaron directly: the priests must not drink wine or strong drink when they enter the tent, and they must teach the people the difference between holy and common, clean and unclean. The chapter ends with Moses angry that a sin offering was burned, not eaten, and Aaron's answer, which pleases Moses.

This is one of the hardest scenes in Leviticus. The text says only that the fire was not commanded, and it does not explain more. Some readers link the warning about wine that follows, but the text does not say that this was the reason. Jewish and Christian interpreters have offered different readings, and it is honest to say that the explanation is not given. The chapter shows that approaching God is serious, and that grief and duty could collide.

God speaks to Moses and Aaron about what Israel may eat. On land, an animal that has a parted hoof and chews the cud may be eaten. The camel, the hyrax and the hare chew the cud but do not part the hoof, and the pig parts the hoof but does not chew the cud, so these are unclean. In the water, whatever has fins and scales may be eaten, and the rest is an abomination. A list of birds follows, including the eagle, vulture, raven, owl, stork and bat. Winged insects are unclean, though locusts, katydids, crickets and grasshoppers may be eaten. The chapter then explains what touching a carcass does: a person is unclean until evening and washes his clothes. At the center of the chapter, God gives the reason: “be holy, for I am holy.” The law, the chapter ends, is to make a distinction between the unclean and the clean.

Why these animals? The text does not give reasons beyond holiness, and many theories have been proposed, such as health, symbolism or setting Israel apart. Jewish tradition has kept these laws as part of daily life. Christians differ on whether they still apply. Many point to Mark 7 and Acts 10 as showing a change, while others see lasting wisdom in them. The uncleanness here is ritual, not a statement that people or animals are evil.

A short chapter, and it concerns birth. When a woman bears a son, she is unclean for seven days, as in the days of her period, and on the eighth day the boy is circumcised. She then continues in the blood of purification for thirty-three days, during which she may not touch any holy thing or come into the sanctuary. If she bears a daughter, the times are doubled: two weeks of uncleanness and sixty-six days of purification. When the days are completed, she brings a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or turtledove for a sin offering. The priest offers it, makes atonement, and she is clean from the flow of her blood. If she cannot afford a lamb, two turtledoves or two young pigeons will do, one for each offering, and she shall be clean.

The uncleanness in this chapter is ritual. It marks a time when a woman keeps apart from the sanctuary and does not say that birth is sinful. Readers differ on why a sin offering is named, and why the time doubles for a daughter; the text does not explain either. The provision for the poor appears again, and Luke 2:22 to 24 records Mary bringing the offering for those who could not afford a lamb. The chapter should be read with care, and it gives no medical advice.

A person finds a swelling, a scab or a bright spot on the skin, and must go to the priest. The priest looks closely: has the hair turned white, does it lie deeper than the skin, has it spread? Some cases he declares unclean at once. In others he isolates the person for seven days and looks again, and if the spot has faded, he pronounces the person clean, and the person washes his clothes. The chapter works through boils, burns, itches of the head and beard, harmless rashes, and baldness. One who is declared leprous must live apart: he wears torn clothes, lets his hair hang loose, covers his upper lip and cries “Unclean! Unclean!” His home is outside the camp. The chapter then turns to mildew in garments of wool, linen or leather, which the priest examines, isolates, and, if it spreads, burns.

The word translated leprosy here covers a range of skin conditions, and many scholars think it is not the same as the modern disease of that name. The priest's job in this chapter is to examine and decide, not to heal. The chapter has often been misused to justify cruel treatment of sick people, and it should not be read that way. It gives no medical advice. See Leviticus 14 for what follows, and Mark 1:40 to 45 for Jesus meeting such a person.

Now the other side: the skin disease has healed. The person is brought to the priest outside the camp. Two living birds, cedar wood, scarlet and hyssop are taken. One bird is killed over running water, the living bird is dipped in its blood, and the priest sprinkles the person seven times, pronounces him clean and lets “the living bird go into the open field.” The person washes, shaves and bathes, waits seven days outside his tent, and on the eighth day brings offerings. The chapter makes room for those who are poor: “If he is poor, and can’t afford so much,” he brings less. Then it turns to a house with spreading mildew. The priest has it emptied and shut up for seven days. If the plague spreads, stones are removed, and if it returns, the house is torn down; if not, it is cleansed with birds and running water.

After the exclusion of Leviticus 13, this chapter is about return: a person coming back into the camp and the worship of Israel. The ritual is long, and every step is a movement toward restored life with others. The law once again provides for the poor. As in chapter 13, the word translated leprosy covers several conditions, and the chapter gives no medical advice. Jesus tells people he heals to show themselves to the priest, as in Luke 17:14.

Some uncleanness in Israel had nothing to do with wrongdoing. It came with the body itself, and Leviticus 15 walks through it patiently. A man with a bodily discharge is unclean, and so is his bed, and so is whatever he sits on, even a saddle. Whoever touches these things washes his clothes, bathes, and is unclean until evening. A clay vessel he touches must be broken.

When the discharge ends, he counts seven days and bathes in running water. On the eighth day he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons to the priest, one for a sin offering and one for a burnt offering. The chapter then turns to an emission of semen, then to a woman's monthly period and to a longer flow of blood. The same pattern of washing, waiting and offering follows each case.

The LORD speaks to Moses and Aaron at Sinai, and this chapter closes the long run of laws about clean and unclean that begins in Leviticus 11. The reason is given at the end: the camp holds the tabernacle, and the people must not “defile my tabernacle that is among them.” Many scholars read these laws as rules about who may approach the sanctuary, not as a verdict on anyone's character. Christians read them in different ways. For one New Testament scene that touches the subject, see Mark 5.

The chapter opens in the shadow of a funeral. Two sons of Aaron had come near the LORD and died, and now the LORD tells Moses that Aaron must not enter the Most Holy Place at just any time, lest he die. When he does enter, it is once a year, in plain linen garments, after bathing. He brings a bull for himself and his house, and carries a censer of burning coals and incense so that a cloud covers the mercy seat.

Two goats stand at the tent door. Lots are cast: one goat for the LORD, one for the scapegoat. The first is offered. Aaron lays both hands on the live goat, confesses the sins of Israel over it, and a man leads it into the wilderness. The day is the tenth of the seventh month, a Sabbath of rest, kept by native and stranger alike.

This is the Day of Atonement, and the opening line ties it to the deaths told in Leviticus 10: nearness to the holy is dangerous and must be approached as the LORD directs. The chapter sits at the center of Leviticus. Jews have kept this day as Yom Kippur. Christians have long read the chapter alongside the book of Hebrews, especially Hebrews 9 and 10. Traditions differ on how the two goats relate to each other and on what atonement means.

Blood is the subject here, and the chapter treats it as something close to sacred. Any Israelite who kills a bull, lamb or goat must bring it to the door of the Tent of Meeting, or be held guilty of shed blood and cut off from the people. The aim is plain: the sacrifices once made in the open field are to be brought to the LORD, and no more offered to goat idols.

Then comes the reason that echoes through the Bible: “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” God has given blood on the altar to make atonement. So no Israelite and no foreigner living among them may eat blood. A hunter pours out the blood of a clean animal and covers it with dust. The chapter ends with a rule about eating what died of itself or was torn by animals.

The LORD speaks to Moses, to Aaron and his sons, and to all Israel. The chapter follows the Day of Atonement in Leviticus 16 and begins the section many scholars call the Holiness Code, which runs through chapter 26. Its teaching on blood is the background for later debates about eating blood, including the decision of the early church in Acts 15. Christians differ on how far these food laws still apply. Jews have kept the laws about blood in their own tradition.

Two lands stand behind this chapter: Egypt, where Israel had lived, and Canaan, where they were going. The LORD says plainly that they must not do as the people of either land do. They are to walk in his ordinances, and “he shall live in them.”

What follows is a long list of forbidden unions. It names close relatives by one title after another: mother, father's wife, sister, granddaughter, aunt, daughter-in-law, brother's wife. It forbids marrying a woman and her sister while the sister lives, and sex with a neighbor's wife. It forbids giving children to Molech. It forbids a man lying with a man as with a woman, and sex with an animal. The warning at the end is stark: the nations before them defiled the land, and the land “vomited out her inhabitants.” Israel must not follow.

The LORD speaks to Moses for all Israel, and the chapter belongs to the Holiness Code that begins in Leviticus 17. The laws are addressed mainly to men and set out limits for the household and for the land. Christians differ on how the verse about two men applies today, and many hold that Jesus and the apostles shape how all these laws are read; see Mark 7 and Acts 15. Many readers also note that the list protects family members from abuse of power.

Here the voice of Leviticus becomes a voice about ordinary life. The LORD tells Moses to speak to the whole congregation: “You shall be holy; for I, the LORD your God, am holy.” Holiness is then spelled out in small, concrete acts. Honor your mother and father. Keep the Sabbaths. Leave the corners of your field and the fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner. Do not steal, lie or swear falsely. Do not hold back a hired worker's pay overnight. Do not curse the deaf or put a stumbling block before the blind.

Judge fairly, without favor to poor or great. Do not slander, hate, or take vengeance, but “you shall love your neighbor as yourself.” The foreigner is to be loved the same way, because Israel was once a foreigner in Egypt. Honest scales close the chapter.

The LORD speaks to Moses at Sinai, and this chapter is the heart of the Holiness Code. Its call to love a neighbor is picked up by Jesus in Mark 12 and by Paul in Romans 13. Some of its rules are hard to place today, such as the mixed fabrics, the haircut rules, and the ruling about a slave girl pledged to another man in verse 20. Christians differ on which laws still bind them and why; the early church looked at this question in Acts 15.

The LORD now attaches penalties to laws given earlier, and the sentences are severe. Giving a child to Molech is punished by stoning, and the LORD says he will set his face against anyone who looks away. Turning to mediums and wizards brings the same warning. Cursing a father or mother, adultery, and several forbidden sexual unions carry the death penalty. Some are punished by being cut off or by childlessness.

Between the verdicts the LORD returns to a plea. “Sanctify yourselves therefore, and be holy”. Israel is not to walk in the customs of the nation being driven out. The LORD has promised them a land flowing with milk and honey, and has set them apart from the peoples. The chapter ends with a ruling on mediums and wizards.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and the chapter belongs with Leviticus 18 as part of the Holiness Code. It is among the hardest chapters in the Bible: many offenses are punished by death. Many scholars note that the Bible gives few cases of these penalties being carried out. Christians read it in different ways, and many point to Jesus' response to the woman caught in adultery in John 8 and to Paul's teaching in Romans 6. The chapter should be read in the setting of ancient Israel's covenant.

The people closest to the holy are held to the strictest rules, and this chapter is about them. The LORD tells Moses to speak to the priests, the sons of Aaron. A priest must not make himself unclean by touching the dead, except for his nearest family. He must not shave his head or cut his flesh, and must not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman. If a priest's daughter profanes herself by prostitution, she is burned.

The high priest is held to still more: he must not let his hair hang loose, tear his clothes, or go near any dead body, even for his father or mother, and he must marry a virgin of his own people. Then comes a hard list. No descendant of Aaron with a defect, such as blindness, lameness or a damaged limb, may offer the bread of God. He may still eat of the holy food.

The LORD speaks to Moses about the priests, who offer the sacrifices and stand closest to the sanctuary. Later in the Bible, the priesthood and its duties shape how people understand holiness; see Hebrews 7 and 1 Peter 2. Many readers find the rules about bodily defects painful. Notice that the text lets such a man share in the holy food. Christians and Jews read the passage differently, and many read it as a picture of the high standard of those who serve.

Holy things are not to be treated lightly, and the chapter begins with a warning to Aaron and his sons: separate yourselves from the holy gifts of Israel when you are unclean, so that they not profane the LORD's name. A priest's descendant who has a skin disease or a discharge may not eat the holy food until he is clean. Washing and waiting until sunset ends the matter.

The chapter also names who may eat. A stranger or hired servant may not. A slave bought with the priest's money may, and so may those born in his house. A priest's daughter who marries an outsider may not, but if she returns widowed or divorced and childless, she may.

Then the focus shifts to the offerings themselves. An animal offered to the LORD must be without defect. The chapter closes with a call to keep the commands.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and the chapter continues the rules for priests that begin in Leviticus 21. The rules for the offering animals match those for the priests: what comes near the altar is to be whole. The chapter assumes slavery, which the Bible does not condemn here; many readers find that hard. The closing words recall the exodus: the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt to be their God. See Exodus 12 and Hebrews 9 for related themes.

The year in Israel is a calendar of meetings with God, and this chapter lays it out. The LORD calls them his “set feasts.” The Sabbath comes first, every seventh day. Then the Passover, on the fourteenth day of the first month in the evening, followed by seven days of unleavened bread.

When the harvest begins, the people bring a sheaf of first fruits to the priest. They count seven Sabbaths, then fifty days, and bring a new offering of two loaves baked with yeast. Twice the chapter says to leave the field's corners for the poor and the foreigner.

In the seventh month come the day of trumpets, the Day of Atonement on the tenth, and on the fifteenth the feast of booths. For seven days the people live in temporary shelters, so that every generation may know how the LORD brought them out of Egypt.

The LORD speaks to Moses and gives the yearly festivals of Israel, each with its own offerings and rest. Jews still keep many of these days. Christians have seen the Passover in the death of Christ and the day fifty days after first fruits in the events of Acts 2. They differ on how far these festivals remain binding on believers; see Colossians 2 and John 7 for two New Testament passages that touch on them.

The chapter opens with light and bread. The people bring pure olive oil so that a lamp burns continually, and Aaron tends it from evening to morning. Twelve cakes of fine flour are set out in two rows on the gold table every Sabbath, with frankincense, and the bread is eaten by Aaron and his sons in a holy place.

Then the scene changes sharply. In the camp, the son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father fights with an Israelite man, and he curses the Name. They hold him in custody until the LORD's will is made known. The LORD says he is to be taken outside the camp and stoned by all the congregation.

The LORD then states the law for all: a killer is put to death, injury is answered with equal injury, and there is “one kind of law for the foreigner as well as the native-born”.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and the chapter joins ritual care of the tabernacle with a case of blasphemy and a statement of justice. The lamp and bread recall Exodus 25. The words “eye for eye” appear again in Matthew 5, where Jesus speaks to those who heard it. Many scholars read the rule as a limit on revenge, setting a measure for what the court may do. Christians read the story of the blasphemer in different ways.

The land itself is given a Sabbath. When Israel enters the land, they are to sow and prune for six years, and in the seventh the land rests: no sowing, no pruning, and what grows of itself is food for everyone. After seven times seven years, on the Day of Atonement, a trumpet sounds in the fiftieth year and liberty is proclaimed throughout the land. This is the jubilee. Each person returns to their own property and family.

The LORD promises a blessing of grain in the sixth year to carry them through. Land is never sold forever, because “the land is mine” A poor relative's land can be redeemed by a kinsman. A poor brother may not be charged interest. An Israelite who sells himself must serve as a hired worker, not a slave, and go free at the jubilee.

Foreign slaves, however, may be kept and inherited. That is a hard line in the text.

The LORD speaks to Moses on Mount Sinai, and the chapter sets out a rhythm of rest and release for the land and the poor. Some scholars question whether the jubilee was kept in practice. Jesus reads from Isaiah in Luke 4, in words that recall this proclaiming of liberty. The permission to hold foreign slaves is one of the Bible's hardest laws, and Christians have used it wrongly; many also point to the way the New Testament speaks of slaves and masters, as in Philemon.

The chapter begins with two commands, no idols and keep my Sabbaths, and then lays two roads before Israel. On the first road the rains come in season, the land gives its increase, the people eat to the full and lie down without fear. The LORD says he will walk among them. “you will be my people”. He reminds them that he broke the bars of their yoke in Egypt.

On the second road, the LORD warns of terror, failed harvests, defeat and plague. Four times he says that if they still do not listen, the punishment grows sevenfold. At the worst the cities are laid waste and the people are scattered. Even the famine is described in horror.

But the chapter does not end in ruin. If they confess and humble their hearts, the LORD will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac and Abraham.

The LORD speaks at Sinai, and this chapter closes the Holiness Code with promised blessings and curses, much as Deuteronomy 28 does later. Many scholars think its picture of exile reflects what Israel later knew, though the text itself presents it as spoken at Sinai. Christians and Jews alike have read the hope of the last verses as a promise that God does not abandon his people. The chapter is hard reading; the point stated is that the LORD will not utterly reject them.

The last chapter of Leviticus is about promises. What if a person vowed to give someone, or something, to the LORD? The text sets a price list. A man from twenty to sixty is valued at fifty shekels of silver, a woman at thirty. Younger and older people have lower prices. If someone is too poor, the priest sets a value according to what he can pay.

The same care covers animals, houses and fields. A person who wishes to buy back what he has given adds a fifth. A field is valued by how many years remain until the jubilee. The firstborn animals already belong to the LORD and cannot be vowed. The tithe of grain, fruit and herd is holy. At the end, the writer notes these are the commandments the LORD gave Moses for Israel on Mount Sinai.

The LORD speaks to Moses, and this short chapter gathers rules about vows and gifts to the sanctuary. It ends the book of Leviticus with a note that all these laws came at Sinai. The valuations are not a statement of a person's worth; they are a payment in place of service, and the text gives mercy to the poor. Many readers see a link between this chapter and the jubilee in Leviticus 25. For a later story of a vow, see Judges 11.
